claim: Sharp-wave ripples (SWR) are transient, 100–250 Hz, local field potential oscillations.
source: More specifically, replay of recent hippocampal patterns has been shown to be concentrated in SWR bursts (transient, 100–250 Hz, local field potential oscillations) and that SWRs significantly predict reactivation of neocortical ensembles during up-states (Peyrache et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as a definition of SWRs, supported by citation to Peyrache et al., 2009.

claim: Post-training, closed-loop interruption of SWR has a negative effect on memory for tasks that normally depend on the hippocampus for acquisition.
source: Finally, post-training, closed-loop interruption of SWR has a negative effect on memory for tasks that normally depend on the hippocampus for acquisition (Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010; Girardeau et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is directly stated and supported by citations to Ego-Stengel and Wilson, 2010 and Girardeau et al., 2009.

claim: A prevalent model is that SWRs arise 'spontaneously' in CA3 and propagate outward to the neocortex through CA1.
source: A prevalent model is that SWRs arise 'spontaneously' in CA3, which could lead to memory retrieval due to attractor network dynamic, and propagate outward to the neocortex through CA1 to enable memory consolidation there (Buzsáki, 1989; Csicsvari et al., 2000; Shen and McNaughton, 1996).
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a prevalent model in the field, supported by multiple citations.

claim: Urethane anesthesia produces a state that is in many respects similar to natural sleep.
source: We combined wide-field optical imaging of dorsal neocortex of mice, covering most of sensory and motor cortices and some association areas, with concurrent electrophysiological monitoring of hippocampal SWRs and MUA during natural sleep and under urethane anesthesia, which produces a state that is in many respects similar to natural sleep (Barthó et al., 2014; Clement et al., 2008; Pagliardini et al., 2013b).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Barthó et al., 2014; Clement et al., 2008; Pagliardini et al., 2013b.

claim: Characteristic electrophysiological signatures of slow-wave sleep including up- and down-states, delta waves, spindles, and hippocampal SWR are present under urethane anesthesia.
source: In particular, characteristic electrophysiological signatures of slow-wave sleep (SWS) including up- and down-states, delta waves, spindles, and hippocampal SWR are present under urethane anesthesia (Barthó et al., 2014; Clement et al., 2008; Pagliardini et al., 2013a; Wolansky et al., 2006; Figure 1Cii; Figure 1—video 1).
evidence: This is explicitly stated and supported by multiple citations and references to figures.

claim: The largest SWR-related modulation occurs in retrosplenial cortex.
source: Using voltage and extracellular glutamate transient recording over widespread regions of mice dorsal neocortex in relation to CA1 multiunit activity (MUA) and SWR, we find that the largest SWR-related modulation occurs in retrosplenial cortex
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Neocortical activation exhibited a continuum of activation timings relative to SWRs, varying from leading to lagging.
source: however, contrary to the unidirectional hypothesis, neocortical activation exhibited a continuum of activation timings relative to SWRs, varying from leading to lagging.
evidence: This is explicitly stated in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: Neocortical activation often precedes SWRs.
source: Thus, contrary to the model in which SWRs arise 'spontaneously' in the hippocampus, neocortical activation often precedes SWRs and may thus constitute a trigger event in which neocortical information seeds associative reactivation of hippocampal 'indices'.
evidence: This is directly stated in the abstract as a finding from the study.

claim: Reactivation of older, more consolidated memories may initiate the hippocampal-neocortical dialog.
source: This timing continuum is consistent with a dynamics in which older, more consolidated memories may in fact initiate the hippocampal-neocortical dialog, whereas reactivation of newer memories may be initiated predominantly in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the timing continuum findings.

claim: Reactivation of newer memories may be initiated predominantly in the hippocampus.
source: This timing continuum is consistent with a dynamics in which older, more consolidated memories may in fact initiate the hippocampal-neocortical dialog, whereas reactivation of newer memories may be initiated predominantly in the hippocampus.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the timing continuum findings.

claim: ~250 ms before the center of SWRs, most neocortical regions transiently deactivated.
source: ~250 ms before the center of SWRs (t = 0; see Materials and methods), most neocortical regions transiently deactivated.
evidence: This is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: Deactivation was followed by a strong activation in most regions in close temporal proximity to SWRs.
source: Deactivation was followed by a strong activation in most regions in close temporal proximity to SWRs (Figure 2A–B).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to figures.

claim: RSC was the most strongly modulated region, showing the highest peak of activation and second highest peak of deactivation.
source: Out of all imaged regions, RSC was the most strongly modulated, showing the highest peak of activation (Figure 3—figure supplement 3Ci) and second highest peak of deactivation (Figure 2—figure supplement 3Cii).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by references to figure supplements.

claim: Regions with comparable magnitudes of activations and deactivations tended to fall within previously identified neocortical structural subnetworks.
source: Interestingly, regions with comparable magnitudes of activations and deactivations tended to fall within previously identified neocortical structural subnetworks (Zingg et al., 2014; Figure 2Ci).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Zingg et al., 2014 and reference to a figure.

claim: The medial subnetwork that includes RSC and posterior parietal cortex along with the visual subnetwork showed the highest degrees of peri-SWR activation.
source: The medial subnetwork that includes RSC and posterior parietal cortex (PtA) along with the visual subnetwork showed the highest degrees of peri-SWR activation (Figure 2Cii–iii; n = 14 per subnetwrok; repeated measure ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction for sphericity: F3,39 = 44.303, p=2.2193 × 10−10; post-hoc multiple comparison with Tuckey's correction: medial vs visual p=0.11844, medial vs auditory p=7.8147 × 10−5, medial vs somatomotor p=1.1128 × 10−6, visual vs auditory p=0.00024702, visual vs somatomotor p=2.9247 × 10−05, auditory vs somatomotor p=0.19802)
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from ANOVA and post-hoc tests.

claim: Ripple power increased most around peak activations in the visual and medial compared with auditory and somatomotor subnetworks.
source: Ripple power increased most around peak activations in the visual and medial compared with auditory and somatomotor subnetworks (Figure 3C; n = 14 per subnetwrok; repeated measure ANOVA with Greenhouse-Geisser correction for sphericity: F3,39 = 14.172, p=1.8183 × 10−5; post-hoc multiple comparison with Tuckey's correction: medial vs visual p=0.99476, medial vs auditory p=0.073032 [p=0.0152 without Greenhouse-Geisser correction], medial vs somatomotor p=0.00054029, visual vs auditory p=0.030248, visual vs somatomotor p=0.0010466, auditory vs somatomotor p=0.17794).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from ANOVA and post-hoc tests.

claim: Hippocampal ripple power is suppressed before the onset of neocortical up-states and elevated after.
source: We found that hippocampal ripple power is suppressed (elevated) before (after) the onset of neocortical up-states.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Hippocampal ripple power is elevated before the onset of neocortical down-states and suppressed after.
source: Similarly, hippocampal ripple power is elevated (suppressed) before (after) the onset of neocortical down-states.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the study.

claim: A medial to lateral temporal gradient in peak times was observed across neocortical regions.
source: A medial to lateral temporal gradient in peak times was observed across neocortical regions (Figure 4Aii; repeated measure ANOVA: F8,104 = 8.357195, p<0.0001; post-hoc test for linear trend: slope = 0.003252024 s/region, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from ANOVA and linear trend test.

claim: Around SWRs, the waves of activity in medial neocortical regions showed the strongest medio-lateral directional component.
source: We observed that around SWRs, the waves of activity in medial neocortical regions showed the strongest medio-lateral directional component, and the strength of this directionality decreased in more lateral regions (Figure 4B; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by references to figures.

claim: On average, neocortical voltage and glutamate activity tended to peak before SWRs in almost all of the imaged regions.
source: On average, neocortical voltage and glutamate activity tended to peak before SWRs in almost all of the imaged regions (Figure 4Aii).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure.

claim: The timings of RSC peak activity relative to SWRs forms a continuum spanning from negative (before) to positive (after) values.
source: Investigation on an individual SWR basis showed that the timings of RSC peak activity relative to SWRs forms a continuum spanning from negative (before) to positive (after) values (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement.

claim: When neocortical activity tended to precede the SWRs there was a buildup of hippocampal MUA preceding the SWRs as well.
source: Interestingly, when neocortical activity tended to precede the SWRs there was a buildup of hippocampal MUA preceding the SWRs as well, whereas when the neocortex activation followed the SWRs, the hippocampal MUA likewise followed.
evidence: This is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: When the neocortex activation followed the SWRs, the hippocampal MUA likewise followed.
source: Interestingly, when neocortical activity tended to precede the SWRs there was a buildup of hippocampal MUA preceding the SWRs as well, whereas when the neocortex activation followed the SWRs, the hippocampal MUA likewise followed.
evidence: This is directly stated as an observation from the data.

claim: The HPC AI values for SWRs in RSC QR1 were less than those for SWRs in RSC QR4.
source: In other words, the HPC AI values for SWRs in RSC QR1 were less than those for SWRs in RSC QR4, and the HPC AI values for SWRs in RSC QR1 and RSC QR4 were more negative and positive, respectively (Figure 5Bii–v; n = 14 per group in Figure 5Bv; one-sided paired Wilcoxon signed-rank test; RSC QR1 versus RSC QR4 p=6.103 × 10−5).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

claim: 55% (median) of peri-SWR RSC activity across animals have negative AI, meaning that on average, neocortical tendency to activate prior to hippocampal SWRs is greater than chance.
source: 55% (median, indicated by a red line) of peri-SWR RSC activity across animals have negative AI, meaning that on average, neocortical tendency to activate prior to hippocampal SWRs is greater than chance (n = 14; one-sided one-sample Wilcoxon signed-rank test; the median is greater than 0.5 with p=1.831 × 10−4).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from Wilcoxon signed-rank test.

claim: On average, only ~ 61% of SWRs have sign-matched RSC and HPC MUA AI values.
source: We found that, on average, only ~ 61% of SWRs have sign-matched RSC and HPC MUA AI values (Figure 6Aii; significantly above the chance level of 50%; two-sided Wilcoxon signed rank test p=1.220703125 × 10−4).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from Wilcoxon signed rank test.

claim: The correlation coefficient between HPC MUA and RSC AI values was low but significant (r = ~0.3).
source: Moreover, the correlation coefficient between HPC MUA and RSC AI values was low but significant (r = ~0.3; n = 11725; two-sided t-test p<10−15; Figure 6Aiii).
evidence: This is directly stated with statistical support from t-test.

claim: SWRs, preceded or followed by MUA (HPC QR1 vs QR4), were similarly preceded or followed by RSC activity, respectively.
source: We found that SWRs, preceded or followed by MUA (HPC QR1 vs QR4), were similarly preceded or followed by RSC activity, respectively (Figure 6Aiv-v; Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by references to figures.

claim: Elevation of hippocampal MUA is correlated with neocortical activation independent of the timestamp at which SRWs occur.
source: Thus, these results suggest that elevation of hippocampal MUA is correlated with neocortical activation independent of the timestamp at which SRWs occur.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the results.

claim: The occasional occurrence of 'bundle' of two or more SWRs was another factor correlating with peri-SWR neocortical activity latency.
source: We found that the occasional occurrence of 'bundle' of two or more SWRs (Davidson et al., 2009; Wu and Foster, 2014) was another factor correlating with peri-SWR neocortical activity latency (Figure 7; Figure 7—figure supplement 1; Figure 7—video 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations and references to figures.

claim: On average, neocortex stayed active for a longer time and peaked later around the bundled than single/isolated ripples.
source: On average, neocortex stayed active for a longer time and peaked later around the bundled than single/isolated ripples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The neocortical deactivation preceding SWRs was stronger in bundled than isolated ripples.
source: Interestingly, the neocortical deactivation preceding SWRs was stronger in bundled than isolated ripples, pointing to the strength of neocortical down-states as a predictor of occurrence of bundled ripples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1Dii).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The neocortical activation was stronger around bundled than isolated ripples.
source: Moreover, the neocortical activation was stronger around bundled than isolated ripples (Figure 7—figure supplement 1Cii).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The inter-SWR time interval distribution of SWRs occurrence was well modeled by an exponential curve only for intervals longer than ~ 250 ms (single/isolated ripples).
source: The inter-SWR time interval distribution of SWRs occurrence was well modeled by an exponential curve (linear curve in logarithmic scale) only for intervals longer than ~ 250 ms (single/isolated ripples).
evidence: This is directly stated as an observation from the data analysis.

claim: For shorter intervals (bundled ripples), there was an excess of positive residuals of the fitted exponential curve.
source: However, for shorter intervals (bundled ripples), there was an excess of positive residuals of the fitted exponential curve (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement.

claim: The mechanisms of SWR generation when they occur in close temporal proximity to each other obeys a non-Poisson dynamic, constituting a different random process from that of single/isolated ripple events.
source: This suggests that the mechanisms of SWR generation when they occur in close temporal proximity to each other obeys a non-Poisson dynamic, constituting a different random process from that of single/isolated ripple events.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the residual analysis.

claim: RSC may mediate the initial information flow from neocortex to hippocampus, probably through entorhinal cortex.
source: Therefore, RSC, which is the first among dorsal neocortical regions to activate around SWRs, may mediate this initial information flow, probably through entorhinal cortex, and subsequently bridge the broadcast of hippocampal index code to the rest of the neocortical mantle.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: The pattern of structural connectivity of RSC with entorhinal cortex and hippocampus supports the idea that RSC mediates information flow.
source: In fact, the pattern of structural connectivity of RSC with entorhinal cortex and hippocampus (Wyss and Van Groen, 1992) supports this idea, where numerous efferents from RSC to entorhinal cortex, the principal input zone to hippocampus, and ample afferents from subicular structure, the main output gate in hippocampus, to RSC have been reported (Amaral and Witter, 1989).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citations to Wyss and Van Groen, 1992 and Amaral and Witter, 1989.

claim: The observed temporal diversity in hippocampal-neocortical interactions around SWRs could reflect the degree of consolidation of a given memory.
source: We speculate that the observed temporal diversity in hippocampal-neocortical interactions around SWRs could reflect the degree of consolidation of a given memory, where neocortex leads hippocampus for well-consolidated memories and lags for newly formed ones.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as speculation by the authors.

claim: Reactivation of recently formed memory traces tend to happen during SWRs around which neocortex follows hippocampus.
source: Our prediction is that reactivation of recently formed memory traces tend to happen during SWRs around which neocortex follows hippocampus.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a prediction by the authors.

claim: The majority of SWRs propagate less than 3 mm across the septal-intermediate or intermediate-temporal portion of the rat hippocampus with a minimum speed of 0.33 mm/ms.
source: The majority of SWRs propagate less than 3 mm across the septal-intermediate or intermediate-temporal portion of the rat hippocampus with a minimum speed of 0.33 mm/ms (Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Patel et al., 2013.

claim: It would take less than 9 ms (equivalent to one cycle of ripples) for SWRs to reach to the electrode tip from their initiation zones.
source: Considering the lengths of mouse hippocampus septal-intermediate and intermediate-temporal portions (~3.25 mm) (Milior et al., 2016), it would take less than 9 ms (equivalent to one cycle of ripples) for SWRs to reach to the electrode tip from their initiation zones.
evidence: This is stated as a calculation based on cited data from Milior et al., 2016.

claim: Changing the location of the electrode tip in the septal-intermediate portion of the hippocampus would have a minimal effect on the results reported in this study.
source: Therefore, changing the location of the electrode tip in the septal-intermediate portion of the hippocampus would have a minimal effect on the results reported in this study.
evidence: This is stated as an inference from the propagation speed calculation.

claim: SWRs in dorsal and ventral portions of the hippocampus often do not co-occur.
source: However, our findings could have been different had we recorded from the intermediate-temporal portion of HPC since SWRs in dorsal and ventral portions of the hippocampus often do not co-occur (Patel et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated and supported by citation to Patel et al., 2013.

claim: Reactivation of prolonged sequences of place cells, encoding recently traversed long routes by rats, tends to occur during bundled ripples.
source: It has been reported that reactivation of prolonged sequences of place cells, encoding recently traversed long routes by rats, tends to occur during bundled ripples (Davidson et al., 2009; Wu and Foster, 2014).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Davidson et al., 2009 and Wu and Foster, 2014.

claim: An isolated ripple has a limited duration and therefore its neural content consists of a sequence of limited number of place cells with place fields covering routes with a limited length.
source: An isolated ripple has a limited duration and therefore its neural content consists of a sequence of limited number of place cells with place fields covering routes with a limited length (Davidson et al., 2009).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Davidson et al., 2009.

claim: The probability of occurrence of a bundled ripple in hippocampus is correlated with the pre-SWR deactivation amplitude in neocortex.
source: Interestingly, according to our data, the probability of occurrence of a bundled ripple in hippocampus is correlated with the pre-SWR (not peri-SWR) deactivation amplitude in neocortex.
evidence: This is directly stated as a finding from the data.

claim: RSC is a potential bridge between hippocampus and the rest of neocortex.
source: Our results reveal neocortical hotspots mediating the broadcast of hippocampal representations to the rest of neocortex by identifying retrosplenial cortex as a potential bridge between these two structures.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Information flow tends to be carried along a medial-lateral direction past the RSC.
source: Past the RSC, information flow tends to be carried along a medial-lateral direction, demonstrating the order of recruitment of different neocortical modules, potentially associated with different features of given memory, around SWRs.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Neocortical activation latency around SWRs is informed by hippocampal features including MUA latency as well as the number of ripple events.
source: Lastly, neocortical activation latency around SWRs is informed by hippocampal features including MUA latency as well as the number of ripple events.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The observed spectrum of temporal latencies in activation of hippocampus and neocortex around SWRs possibly reflects the direction of communication during hippocampal and neocortical reactivations of recent versus remote memories.
source: The observed spectrum of temporal latencies in activation of hippocampus and neocortex around SWRs possibly reflects the direction of communication during hippocampal and neocortical reactivations of recent versus remote memories.
evidence: This is stated as an interpretation of the findings.

claim: Encoding of new hippocampal-dependent memories lead to a transient bias toward hippocampus leading neocortex around post-encoding sleep SWRs.
source: We predict that encoding of new hippocampal-dependent memories lead to a transient bias toward hippocampus leading neocortex around post-encoding sleep SWRs and that this bias would last until the load of consolidating new information gradually dissipates.
evidence: This is explicitly stated as a prediction by the authors.

claim: Both VSD and iGluSnFR measures electrical activity with relatively high temporal resolution.
source: Unlike calcium reporters (e.g., GCaMP6) with slow kinetics, both VSD and iGluSnFR measures electrical activity with relatively high temporal resolution (Xie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Xie et al., 2016.

claim: The wide-field optical imaging of membrane potential activity in a given region of interest was correlated with LFP activity recorded from the same neocortical site.
source: The wide-field optical imaging of membrane potential activity in a given region of interest was correlated with LFP activity recorded from the same neocortical site confirming that the optical voltage signal reflects underlying electrophysiological processes (Arieli et al., 1995; Figure 1C).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Arieli et al., 1995 and reference to a figure.

claim: Emx-CaMKII-Ai85 crossing is expected to produce expression of iGluSnFR within all excitatory neurons across all layers of the cortex, but not in GABAergic neurons.
source: This crossing is expected to produce expression of iGluSnFR within all excitatory neurons across all layers of the cortex, but not in GABAergic neurons (Huang and Zeng, 2013; Madisen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citations to Huang and Zeng, 2013 and Madisen et al., 2015.

claim: Brain sections of the positive transgenic mice confirmed robust expression in the neocortex and hippocampus.
source: Brain sections of the positive transgenic mice confirmed robust expression in the neocortex and hippocampus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by reference to a figure supplement showing expression.

claim: Mice slept with eyelids partially open during natural sleep experiments.
source: During the natural sleep experiments, pupil dilation measurement was possible since mice slept with eyelids partially open (Yüzgeç et al., 2018).
evidence: This is directly stated and supported by citation to Yüzgeç et al., 2018.

claim: SWRs detected under urethane anesthesia tend to have slower peak frequencies than those in natural sleep.
source: SWRs detected under urethane anesthesia tend to have slower peak frequencies. The red plus signs represent the data points outside the interval (centered on median value) which includes 99.3 percent of all data points.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B comparing peak spectral frequencies across conditions.

claim: SWRs detected under urethane anesthesia tend to have shorter durations than those in natural sleep.
source: Note that the SWRs detected under urethane anesthesia tend to have shorter durations.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C comparing SWR durations across conditions.

claim: Mean peri-SWR neocortical activity patterns during head-restrained sleep are similar to spatiotemporal patterns obtained under urethane-anesthesia.
source: Mean peri-SWR neocortical activity patterns during head-restrained sleep are similar to spatiotemporal patterns of neocortical deactivation and activation around SWR times obtained under urethane-anesthesia.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: There is no significant difference between peri-SWR activation amplitude trends under urethane anesthesia and natural sleep.
source: As measured by correlation coefficients, there is no significant difference between both activation and deactivation amplitude trends under urethane anesthesia and natural sleep. Therefore, we decided to pool the urethane and natural sleep data in this paper.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 3D.

claim: RSC shows the largest delta power across all regions and animals in electrophysiological recordings during natural sleep.
source: RSC shows the largest delta power across all regions and animals.
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 5C(i).

claim: Medial subnetwork compared to the somatomotor subnetwork receive stronger modulation around hippocampal SWRs in electrophysiological recordings.
source: Grouping the data from four neocortical regions into neocortical subnetworks, defined in Figure 2C i, shows that medial subnetwork compared to the somatomotor subnetwork receive stronger modulation around hippocampal SWRs (p<0.01, one-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test).
evidence: This is stated in the caption of Figure 2—figure supplement 5C(ii) with statistical support.

claim: 62 ± 0.03% (mean + SEM; n = 14 mice) of all detected bundled ripples consist of two ripples.
source: 62 ± 0.03% (mean + SEM; n = 14 mice) of all detected bundled ripples in our data consist of two ripples.
evidence: This is directly stated in the Materials and methods section.
